pos: n. (the Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1180, burial house of the Ascanian margraves, source of the forged Lehnin Prophecy)
etymology: German Lehnin, from a Slavic root for a doe or a clearing, latinised Lenin.
biblical_def: Lehnin in Brandenburg was founded about 1180 by Margrave Otto I and settled from Sittichenbach, and it became the burial house of the Ascanian margraves and the richest monastery in the march. Its brick church survives. Lehnin is also the home of a famous fraud. The Vaticinium Lehninense, a Latin poem of a hundred hexameters attributed to a thirteenth-century monk named Hermann, foretells in careful order the fortunes of Brandenburg and the fall of the Hohenzollerns; it was in fact composed late in the seventeenth century, and was used for two centuries by men who wanted a prophecy to lean on. The dictionary records Lehnin as a lesson in how prophecy is tested. Scripture supplies one measure and refuses to supply another: everything is referred back to a written standard, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20), and the apostolic word is called more sure than even a voice from heaven heard with the ears, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19). A people that will not use the measure drifts by preferring novelty, “they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths” (Jer 18:15), and the apostolic alarm against such borrowed authority is explicit, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prophecy as a foretelling of future events by inspiration; a forgery as the crime of counterfeiting writing; a vaticination as prediction; apocryphal as not canonical, of doubtful authority; and a canon as a rule or law, the genuine books of Scripture.
webster_full: PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come, which human sagacity could not foresee.
FORGERY, n. The crime of counterfeiting; the fraudulent making or alteration of a writing.
VATICINATION, n. Prediction; prophecy.
APOCRYPHAL, adj. Not canonical; of uncertain authority or credit; false; fictitious.
CANON, n. In theology, the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon or rule of faith.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1180, burial house of the Ascanians, and the source of a seventeenth-century forged prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prophecy is tested against a written rule and not against its own plausibility. The Lehnin verses were believed because they were old and gloomy, and the prophet's test cuts straight through both qualities, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

The live temptation is a traffic in private prediction, which was Lehnin's trade and remains a trade. Peter ranks the written word above his own eyewitness of the transfiguration, calling it “a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19); the drift that makes forgeries welcome is a forsaking of the old ways, “Because my people hath forgotten me” (Jer 18:15); and the apostolic guard against borrowed authority names its source, “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8).

pos: n. (the Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1273, a masterpiece of north German brick Gothic, now a roofless ruin)
etymology: German Chorin, from a Slavic place-name, perhaps chor, a thicket.
biblical_def: Chorin north-east of Berlin was founded in 1273 when the Cistercians of Mariensee moved to a better site, and the church they raised there is the finest brick Gothic building of the north German plain: a west front of tall blind arcading and slender turrets built entirely without stone, since the march had no quarries and the monks had clay. It was the Ascanian mausoleum until the line failed. The abbey was dissolved in 1542, served as a farm and a sawmill, lost its roof, and was rescued in the nineteenth century as a Romantic ruin, which is how it stands: walls and tracery open to the sky. The dictionary records Chorin among the ruins because Scripture treats a desolate sanctuary as a thing to mourn and to learn from rather than to admire. The lament over an emptied house is bitter, “The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts” (Lam 1:4), and the psalmist's complaint over a wrecked holy place is a complaint and not an aesthetic, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7). Micah was given to say that even the temple mount would become woodland, “the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest” (Mic 3:12). The hope held out is rebuilding and not picturesque decay, “they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isa 61:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; desolation as destruction, a place wasted; tracery as ornamental stonework in a window; Gothic as pertaining to the pointed style of architecture; and a mausoleum as a magnificent tomb.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, the remains of a decayed or demolished city or house.
DESOLATION, n. The act of deserting or laying waste; a place deserted or laid waste; gloominess; sadness.
TRACERY, n. In architecture, ornamental stone-work, as in the heads of Gothic windows.
GOTHIC, adj. Pertaining to the Goths; denoting the style of architecture with pointed arches.
MAUSOLEUM, n. A magnificent tomb, or stately monument for the dead.
scriptures: Lam 1:4
The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness.
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
Mic 3:12
Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest.
Isa 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
corruption_summary: Brandenburg Cistercian abbey of 1273, the finest brick Gothic church of the north, dissolved 1542 and kept as a roofless ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a ruined house of worship is an occasion for mourning, not for taste. Chorin was saved in the nineteenth century because it looked well without a roof, and the scriptural register for an emptied sanctuary is grief, “all her gates are desolate” (Lam 1:4).

The live temptation is the picturesque, which turns judgment into scenery. The psalmist will not do it; he reports the wreck as an outrage, “they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7). Micah was given to say the same of the temple itself, “Zion for your sake be plowed as a field” (Mic 3:12), and the promise attached to such places is labour and not admiration, “they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4).

pos: n. (the Mecklenburg Cistercian abbey of 1171, burial house of the Mecklenburg dukes, site of a Holy Blood shrine)
etymology: Slavic dobry, good, in the sense of the good place or good water.
biblical_def: Doberan in Mecklenburg was founded in 1171 by Prince Pribislav after his baptism, destroyed in a pagan rising, and refounded in 1186. Its brick minster is the burial church of the Mecklenburg dukes and holds one of the most complete sets of medieval furnishings in northern Europe, including a great cross altar and an octagonal shrine built to display a relic of the Holy Blood. That shrine made Doberan a pilgrimage house and made its fortune. The dictionary records it as the clearest Mecklenburg case of a sanctuary built around the wrong object. The relic trade rested on the assumption that the sacrifice of Christ needs renewing, applying, or localising in a vessel, and the epistle to the Hebrews was written to deny it: the offering was single, and the posture that followed it was sitting down, “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12). Its sufficiency is stated without remainder, “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). Death comes once and then judgment, with no treasury in between, “as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27), and salvation is tied to a name rather than to a shrine, “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a dead body, also what is kept in memory with veneration; a shrine as a case in which sacred things are deposited; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; a reliquary as a depository for relics; and veneration as the highest degree of respect.
webster_full: RELIC, n. The remains of a dead body; also, that which remains; that which is left after the loss of the rest.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle, in which sacred things are deposited; a tomb or altar.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable.
RELIQUARY, n. A casket in which relics are kept; a depository for relics.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
scriptures: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: Mecklenburg Cistercian house of 1171 whose Holy Blood shrine made it a pilgrimage centre and the dukes' burial church.
corruption_paragraphs: Doberan's octagonal shrine was raised to hold a relic of the Holy Blood, and the whole trade it served assumed that what Christ did at Calvary requires continual application through objects. Hebrews was written against that assumption, and its argument turns on a posture: the priests of the old covenant stood daily, but “this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12). A seated priest is a finished work.

The corruption is not merely medieval. Rome's Council of Trent anathematised the doctrine that the mass is a bare memorial and defined it as a true propitiatory sacrifice, which keeps Doberan's logic alive in the altar if not in the reliquary. Scripture closes the account: the offering is complete, “he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14); the sequence after death admits no intervening treasury of merit, “once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27); and the saving instrument is a person named, “Neither is there salvation in any other” (Act 4:12).

Greek onoma (G3686) — a name, the person named; “there is none other name under heaven”, Acts 4:12.

“he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14) — sufficiency without remainder.
“Neither is there salvation in any other” (Act 4:12) — a name, not a shrine.

pos: n. (the Pomeranian Cistercian abbey of 1173, the first of the order in Pomerania, settled from Esrum)
etymology: Slavic Kolbacz, from a personal or water name; German Kolbatz.
biblical_def: Kolbatz on the Plone in Pomerania was founded in 1173 by Duke Warcislaw II and settled by monks from Esrum in Denmark, the first Cistercian house in Pomerania and the mother of Oliva, Marienwalde and Himmelstadt. It was an engine of settlement: the monks drained the lower Plone, laid out villages, built a brick church of cathedral scale, and kept the chronicle that is one of the chief sources for early Pomeranian history. It was dissolved in 1535. The dictionary records Kolbatz for the missionary pattern of the Cistercian advance into the Slavic east, and for the limit of that pattern. Christ's own account of the need is a shortage of workers and not of ground, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and He forbids the delay that always looks reasonable, “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35). The limit is this: men may be settled on land without being converted, and the harvest Scripture means is not a tenancy. Sowing of the true kind costs something, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5), and the law of the field is inescapable for the sower as much as for the soil, “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a harvest as the season of reaping, also the ripe corn gathered; to sow as to scatter seed; a labourer as one who works with the hands; a chronicle as a historical account of facts in order of time; and a daughter-house is a convent founded from another.
webster_full: HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering grain or other crops; also, the ripe corn or grain collected.
SOW, v.t. To scatter seed upon ground for the purpose of growth; to plant by strewing.
LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
COLONIZE, v.t. To plant or establish a colony in; to form into a colony.
scriptures: Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Joh 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: Pomerania's first Cistercian house, 1173, settled from Esrum, mother of Oliva, and an engine of eastward settlement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the harvest is reckoned in converted men and not in settled acres. Kolbatz drained marsh and planted villages, good work in itself, and the Lord's own accounting of the shortage is of workers, “but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37).

The live temptation is to count a Christianised map as a reaped field. Christ refuses the postponement that makes such counting comfortable, “Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest?” (Joh 4:35); the sowing He means is costly, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5); and the law that governs it holds against every institutional cleverness, “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal 6:7).
roots_summary: Greek therismos (G2326), a harvest; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman; Hebrew zara (H2232), to sow; Greek speiro (G4687), to sow seed.

pos: n. (the Pomeranian Hanseatic town and university of 1456, reformed from 1531 under Johannes Knipstro)
etymology: German Greifswald, the griffin's wood, from the Pomeranian griffin and Wald.
biblical_def: Greifswald in Pomerania grew up beside the Cistercian abbey of Eldena, received town law in 1250, joined the Hanse, and in 1456 was given a university, the second-oldest in northern Germany and for centuries the chief school of Pomerania and of Swedish Germany. The Reformation came in 1531, carried by Johannes Knipstro, and the university was reorganised on evangelical lines with the Pomeranian church order that Johannes Bugenhagen, a Pomeranian himself, had drafted for the north. The dictionary records Greifswald for the link between a reformed church and a trained ministry, which the Lutheran church orders treated as one subject. Malachi makes instruction the priest's defining possession, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7), and the promise of restored shepherds is a promise of competent ones, “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15). A church of such pastors produces laymen who can account for what they hold, “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), and the whole enterprise has a starting point that no faculty can supply, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a university as an institution for instruction in all the branches of learning; a faculty as the masters and professors of a science; a matriculation is enrollment in a university; a divine as a minister of the gospel, a theologian; and knowledge as a clear perception of truth.
webster_full: UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
FACULTY, n. The masters and professors of the several sciences in a university, college or seminary.
MATRICULATE, v.t. To enter or admit to membership in a body or society, particularly in a university.
DIVINE, n. A minister of the gospel; a priest; a clergyman; one versed in divinity.
KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact.
scriptures: Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
corruption_summary: Pomeranian Hanse town and university of 1456, reformed in 1531 and reorganised under Bugenhagen's church order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a reformed church needs a taught ministry, and that the two were planned together. Greifswald's university was reorganised in the same decade as its churches, and the prophet makes instruction the minister's defining stock, “they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

The live temptation runs both ways: a learning that outgrows the fear of God, or a piety that despises learning. Scripture refuses each. The pastors promised are men who “feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15); the ordinary layman is expected to “give an answer to every man that asketh you” (1Pe 3:15); and the beginning of the whole business is not a curriculum, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).

pos: n. (the Pomeranian Hanseatic town on the Peene, a brick Gothic trading port)
etymology: German Anklam, from Slavic Tanglim, a personal name; earlier Tanclim.
biblical_def: Anklam on the Peene in Pomerania received town law in 1264, joined the Hanse, and lived by the grain and herring trade through the lagoon to the Baltic. Its brick churches of St Mary and St Nicholas are of the standard Wendish Gothic kind, and its wealth rose and fell with the navigability of the river and the fortunes of Swedish Pomerania; it was burned in the Thirty Years' War, besieged repeatedly, and bombed in the last war. The dictionary records Anklam among the Hanse towns because the merchant's standing is a biblical theme and the merchant town is a standing illustration of it. The patriarchs are described as men who held their tenancy loosely and died holding it, “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), and the apostle addresses Christians under exactly that double title, “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11). A trading town makes the lesson concrete, because its prosperity is visibly on loan, and the psalmist's confession fits any port, “for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Psa 39:12). The conclusion the epistle draws is not retreat from commerce but a corrected expectation, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough with full rights; the Hanse as a league of commercial cities; a staple as a settled mart; a sojourner as a temporary resident; and a pilgrim as a wanderer, one who travels to a distance from home.
webster_full: BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town, or one who possesses a full right of citizenship.
HANSE, n. A society of merchants; the Hanseatic towns were commercial cities in league for protection of trade.
STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; a city or town where certain commodities are chiefly taken for sale.
SOJOURNER, n. A temporary resident; a stranger or traveler who dwells in a place for a time.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: Pomeranian Hanse port on the Peene, chartered 1264, grown and ruined by river trade and war.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that settled prosperity is a tenancy. Anklam's wealth depended on a river that silted and a crown that changed hands, and the patriarchs are commended for holding their ground on exactly those terms, “having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them” (Heb 11:13).

The live temptation is to read the pilgrim language as contempt for trade and towns. Peter does not; he writes to tradesmen and calls them “Dearly beloved” (1Pe 2:11) in the same breath as he calls them strangers. The psalmist's own confession is made to God and not against his neighbours, “Hear my prayer, O LORD” (Psa 39:12), and the conclusion is a corrected expectation rather than a withdrawal, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

“I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11) — written to tradesmen, not to hermits.

pos: n. (the Mecklenburg Cistercian abbey of 1172, dissolved 1552 and rebuilt as a ducal palace)
etymology: Slavic Dargun, from a personal name, perhaps Dargon.
biblical_def: Dargun in Mecklenburg was founded in 1172 from Esrum, destroyed in a pagan rising, refounded in 1209, and grew into a landed house with granges across the Tollense valley. At the Reformation the community was dissolved in 1552, and the dukes of Mecklenburg-Gūstrow did not pull the buildings down but converted them: the conventual ranges became a residence, and over the next century a palace grew out of the cloister, with the abbey church kept as a court chapel. The dictionary records Dargun for the commonest fate of a dissolved abbey in the Protestant north, which is not destruction but absorption into a nobleman's estate, and for the question that fate raises. The transfer of monastic wealth to princely hands was defended as reform and was very often simple appetite. Christ allows no third master, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24), and the apostolic diagnosis names the root exactly, “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10). The Lord's warning is against a reckoning of life by holdings, “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15), and the church at Laodicea shows how invisible such wealth makes its own poverty, “I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing” (Rev 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to secularize as to convert to common use; an appropriation as the act of setting apart for a particular use; mammon as riches, wealth personified; covetousness as an inordinate desire of wealth; and a demesne as a manor-house with the adjoining lands.
webster_full: SECULARIZE, v.t. To convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular or common use.
APPROPRIATION, n. The act of setting apart or assigning to a particular use, in exclusion of all other uses.
MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth; or the god of riches.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good.
DEMESNE, n. A manor-house, and the land adjacent or near, which the lord keeps in his own hands.
scriptures: Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
corruption_summary: Mecklenburg Cistercian house of 1172 dissolved in 1552 and rebuilt as a ducal palace around the old cloister.
corruption_paragraphs: Dargun was not destroyed; it was moved into. The conventual ranges became a palace and the church became a court chapel, and the dukes who arranged it described the transfer as reformation. Some of it was. A great deal of the northern dissolution was appetite wearing the vocabulary of reform, and the Lord's word on the arrangement admits no middle term, “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).

The corruption to name is not only the princes'. The abbeys had themselves grown rich on the theory that endowments purchase masses, so the wealth was corrupt before it changed hands. Paul locates the trouble in an affection rather than in a sum, “which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10); Christ forbids the arithmetic that equates life with holdings, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15); and Laodicea is the standing example of a church that could not see its own condition, “and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Rev 3:17).
roots_summary: Greek mamonas (G3126), riches, wealth; Greek philarguria (G5365), love of money; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness; Greek talaiporos (G5005), wretched.
roots_lines: Greek mamonas (G3126) — riches, wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”, Matthew 6:24.
Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money, avarice; “For the love of money is the root of all evil”, 1 Timothy 6:10.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, a grasping for more; “Take heed, and beware of covetousness”, Luke 12:15.
Greek huparcho (G5225) — to be, to possess, goods on hand; “the things which he possesseth”, Luke 12:15.
Greek talaiporos (G5005) — wretched, afflicted; “thou art wretched, and miserable”, Revelation 3:17.
usage: “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24) — no third master is on offer.
“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — the root is an affection, not a sum.
“I am rich, and increased with goods” (Rev 3:17) — how invisible such wealth makes its poverty.

pos: n. (the Pomeranian Cistercian abbey of 1231, dissolved 1535, whose stones built the town of Franzburg)
etymology: German Neuenkamp, the new field, from neu and Kamp, an enclosed field.
biblical_def: Neuenkamp in western Pomerania was founded in 1231 from Hiddensee's mother house at Neuencamp and became a considerable landowner on the Barth peninsula, founding in turn the island house on Hiddensee. It was dissolved in 1535. Duke Bogislaw XIII then did something unusually frank: he built himself a residence from the abbey and laid out a new town beside it, named Franzburg after his father-in-law, using the conventual buildings as a quarry. The church went into the houses. The dictionary records Neuenkamp for the plainness of that transaction and for the question Scripture puts to every builder. Christ's own prophecy over the temple was that its stones would be taken apart, “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2), so a dismantled sanctuary is not outside the ways of God. But the Lord also requires a reckoning before the first stone is laid, “sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28), and the prophet rebukes exactly the order of priorities Bogislaw followed, a panelled house beside a ruined one, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). When men go silent, the material itself is said to be competent to testify, “the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a quarry as a place where stones are dug; to demolish as to throw down a building; a residence as the place of abode; ceiled as having an inner roof or lining; and a cost as the price of a thing, the expense.
webster_full: QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
DEMOLISH, v.t. To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy; to ruin; applied chiefly to buildings.
RESIDENCE, n. The place of abode; a dwelling; a habitation.
CEILED, pp. Furnished with an inner roof or lining; overlaid with wainscot or plaster.
COST, n. The price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased; expense; charge.
scriptures: Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
corruption_summary: Pomeranian Cistercian house of 1231 dissolved in 1535 and quarried for the duke's residence and the new town of Franzburg.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that stones are not sacred and priorities are. Neuenkamp went into houses, and Christ had already said of a far holier building that its masonry would come apart, “See ye not all these things?” (Mat 24:2), so the dismantling by itself proves nothing either way.

The live temptation is the order Bogislaw chose, which is to finish one's own house first. The Lord requires a reckoning before building begins, “intending to build a tower” (Luk 14:28); Haggai names the sin precisely as panelling a private dwelling while God's house lies waste, “and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4); and where men keep quiet about such things the material is said to be competent to speak, “if these should hold their peace” (Luk 19:40).
roots_summary: Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek psephizo (G5585), to count up, to reckon; Hebrew saphan (H5603), to cover, to panel; Hebrew chareb (H2720), waste, desolate.
roots_lines: Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone, a building stone; “There shall not be left here one stone upon another”, Matthew 24:2.
Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count with pebbles, to reckon up; “counteth the cost”, Luke 14:28.
Greek purgos (G4444) — a tower; “intending to build a tower”, Luke 14:28.
Hebrew saphan (H5603) — to cover in, to panel, to ceil; “to dwell in your cieled houses”, Haggai 1:4.
Greek krazo (G2896) — to cry out, to shriek; “the stones would immediately cry out”, Luke 19:40.
usage: “There shall not be left here one stone upon another” (Mat 24:2) — stones are not the sacred thing.
“and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4) — the order of priorities Haggai rebukes.
“counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28) — the reckoning required before building.

pos: n. (the Baltic island west of Rugen, site of a Cistercian monastery founded 1296 from Neuenkamp)
etymology: Old Norse Hedinsey, Hedin's island, from a personal name and ey, an island.
biblical_def: Hiddensee is a long sandbar island off the west coast of Rūgen, and in 1296 the Cistercians of Neuenkamp planted a monastery there under the dedication of St Nicholas. It was never large: a handful of monks, a church, fishponds and salt pans, cut off by weather for weeks at a time. It was dissolved in 1534 and almost nothing of it stands. The dictionary records Hiddensee as a picture of sought solitude and as a correction to the way solitude is usually defended. The monastic argument for an island was that withdrawal is itself a higher state; the biblical warrant is narrower and better. Christ withdrew, and the texts are careful to say what He withdrew in order to do, “he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35), a habit and not an occasion, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16). The withdrawal was also temporary and followed by return, and it came after service rather than instead of it, “when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray” (Mat 14:23). The end is persistence, which is the one thing a monastery of six men on a sandbar could actually model, “men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solitude as loneliness, a lonely place; to withdraw as to retire, to go back; an eremite as a hermit; a cell as a small close apartment in a monastery; and an island as a tract of land surrounded by water.
webster_full: SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; also, a lonely place, a desert.
WITHDRAW, v.i. To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place.
EREMITE, n. One who lives in a wilderness, or in retirement; a hermit.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison or monastery; a cave; a small religious house.
ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water.
scriptures: Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Luk 5:16
And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.
And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone.
Luk 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
corruption_summary: Baltic sandbar island with a small Cistercian house of 1296, dissolved 1534 and almost wholly gone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that withdrawal is for prayer and is measured by it. Hiddensee's monks were cut off by weather rather than by merit, and the gospel is careful to state the purpose of every retirement it records, “and there prayed” (Mar 1:35).

The live temptation is the old monastic claim that solitude is a higher state in itself, with its modern counterpart that solitude is a technique for the self. Scripture ties it to an act and to a return: the withdrawing was habitual, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16), it came after the crowds were served and not instead of serving them, “And when he had sent the multitudes away” (Mat 14:23), and the point of it all is not depth but endurance, “and not to faint” (Luk 18:1).
roots_summary: Greek eremos (G2048), desert, solitary; Greek proseuchomai (G4336), to pray; Greek hupochoreo (G5298), to withdraw; Greek ekkakeo (G1573), to faint, to lose heart.
roots_lines: Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, solitary, uninhabited; “departed into a solitary place”, Mark 1:35.
Greek proseuchomai (G4336) — to pray, to make request; “and there prayed”, Mark 1:35.
Greek hupochoreo (G5298) — to withdraw, to go back; “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness”, Luke 5:16.
Greek apolyo (G0630) — to send away, to dismiss; “when he had sent the multitudes away”, Matthew 14:23.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to faint, to lose heart; “and not to faint”, Luke 18:1.
usage: “departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) — the stated purpose of every retirement.
“when he had sent the multitudes away” (Mat 14:23) — after service, not instead of it.
“men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1) — what a tiny house could really model.

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon Hanseatic town on the lower Elbe, an early Reformation city with a Benedictine abbey)
etymology: Old Saxon stada, a bank or landing-place, cognate with English staithe.
biblical_def: Stade on the lower Elbe is named for a landing-place, which is what it was: a harbour on the Schwinge a few miles above the river mouth, seat of the counts of Stade, a Hanse member from the thirteenth century, and in later years the capital of Swedish Bremen-Verden. It held the Benedictine abbey of St George and a college of canons, and it went over to the Reformation early, with an evangelical preacher at St Cosmae by 1522. Its trade was in grain, timber and transit dues on the Elbe, and its wealth depended on strangers coming in. The dictionary records Stade among the Hanse towns for the duty that a port makes unavoidable. Hospitality in Scripture is not a courtesy but a command with a reason attached, “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2), and it is listed among the plain marks of a Christian, “Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13). The religion that God approves is defined by whom it visits, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), and the whole requirement is reduced by the prophet to three things, none of them commercial, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a staithe as a landing-place; hospitality as the practice of receiving and entertaining strangers; a guild as a society or corporation; a toll as a tax for passage; and alms as anything given to relieve the poor.
webster_full: STAITH, n. A landing place; an edge or bank, as of a river.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some purpose, particularly of trade.
TOLL, n. A tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for passage over a bridge or on a highway.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon Hanse port on the Elbe, Benedictine abbey of St George, evangelical from 1522, later Swedish Bremen-Verden.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hospitality is commanded and not merely admired. Stade lived by strangers arriving on the tide, and the epistle turns that trade into a duty with a remarkable reason, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).

The live temptation in a prosperous port is to let charity become a guild function and so cease to be personal. The apostolic list keeps it personal and immediate, “Distributing to the necessity of saints” (Rom 12:13); James defines acceptable religion by its object rather than its register, “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this” (Jam 1:27); and Micah reduces the whole requirement to a shape no committee can hold, “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good” (Mic 6:8).
roots_summary: Greek philonexia (G5381), love of strangers, hospitality; Greek xenos (G3581), a stranger; Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to visit, to look after; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy, steadfast love.
roots_lines: Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers”, Hebrews 13:2.
Greek lanthano (G2990) — to be hidden, to be unaware; “entertained angels unawares”, Hebrews 13:2.
Greek koinoneo (G2841) — to share, to have in common; “Distributing to the necessity of saints”, Romans 12:13.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, to look after; “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction”, James 1:27.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, steadfast covenant love; “and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.
usage: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) — a command, not a courtesy.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) — religion defined by its object.
“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — the whole requirement in three terms.
